newsitem.title: HUNGARY: East European markets share worldwide nervousness.
newsitem.headline: East European markets share worldwide nervousness.

text.p: Central and eastern European share markets fell sharply this week as Wall Street, which hit a record high on Tuesday, gave little help to the region's bourses.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which follows price movements in 73 Czech, Polish, Hungarian, Slovak and Slovenian stocks, shed almost two percent.
BUDAPEST

The Hungarian share market tumbled more than seven percent this week and traders, although divided on how long the sluggish period would last, said they expected the underlying trend to remain unchanged.

Many traders believe that a sideways trend will last until the next phase of the privatisation of oil company MOL in May, but there are some who believe that falling prices may encourage new purchases.
"I'm not that pessimistic," said Andrea Keresztesi of ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett (Hungary). "Should the market fall some more it would become attractive again and trigger some rises."
On Friday the BUX index closed at 4,992.45 points, down 388.7 from last Friday.
WARSAW
Polish shares fell 5.7 percent this week and analysts said the market, now at 16,687.1 points, would apparently fall more after having gained 38 percent from mid-December to mid-February.

"There's been no radical overvaluing for us to expect a big correction...but definitely we'll have a correction of about 10 percent to 16,000 points," said Michal Szczurek, an analyst at ING BSK Asset Management.

Analysts said Friday's news of a deeper than expected slide in U.S. wholesale prices, which cheered some Western bourses in the view that U.S. interest rates would remain stable, could lead to growth in Warsaw on Monday.
But they said subsequent falls were still possible.
"I think a lot of investors got scared by the recent big falls and will use a possible rebound to take profits," said Pawel Tarnowski of Raiffeisen Capital and Investment.
PRAGUE

Czech shares moved lower throughout the week with analysts saying foreign investors were becoming increasingly cautious about prospects for Czech equities because of concerns about the country's macroeconomic fundamentals.
"Generally it (the downturn) is caused by lack of demand because there are no new orders from abroad and domestic speculators see no reason to buy," said Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostenska Banka.
"People are just sitting and watching," added Radim Bajgar of ING Barings.
The three most heavily capitalised shares on the PX50 -- SPT Telecom, CEZ and Komercni Banka -- which account for 45 percent of the index's capitalisation dropped by an average of 6.5 percent.
On Friday the PX50 closed at 563.4 points, down 20.3.
BRATISLAVA

The Slovak bourse extended its rally from the past few weeks in the first two days of the week, with the official 16-share SAX index reaching a year high of 207.75 points on Tuesday. But the SAX then retreated and closed at 204.65 on Friday, down 1.33 points from Monday's open.

Brokers said that, despite the drop, the Slovak market appeared unaffected by the current downtrend in the neigbouring countries, adding that the BSE should hold at its current levels, or post a slight increase, in the mid-term.
"Even after including the potential risk of the political situation, our market is still undervalued compared with other bourses in the region," said Libor Briska of Creditanstalt.
"Continuing demand for the most attractive issues, such as refiner Slovnaft or drug maker Slovakofarma could push the SAX again above 207 points."
ZAGREB

Croatian stocks ended the week mixed in slow trade, but traders said the lull was only temporary as the market geared up for further gains. The lull came about as investors became cautious, awaiting results of the local elections set for April 13.
Traders singled out fully-listed Zagrebacka Banka as the most promising issue, which will set the pace for the rest of the market. The bank hit an all-time high on Wednesday.
"Zagrebacka is going sky-high, but we feel there is quite some potential left for further growth," Damir Cikotic of Faktor brokerage said. kuna than a week ago.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares firmed 0.96 percent this week, pushing the SBI index to 1,390.99 points on Friday. Traders expected the market to continue trading with little clear direction.
"The market is desperate for some information concerning future of foreign investments," one trader said.
BUCHAREST
Bucharest bourse turnover edged lower with most stocks falling this week as investor interest continued to dim.
Trading at the week's three sessions was dominated by first-tier Oltchim SA chemical plant and fertiliser maker Azomures SA, with interest in second-tier shares almost absent.
Brokers said several factors, including a firmer leu and high interest rates on banking deposits, combined to cap buying by domestic and foreign investors.
